list-basic.title: Basic List<T> operations
list-basic.summary: List<T> is commonly used for array-like data whose number of elements can change.
list-basic.why: List<T> manages its internal capacity and lets Add and Remove change the element count.
list-basic.tips: Index access is fast, but still make sure the index is within range.

list-filter.title: Filter a List by condition
list-filter.short: Use Where to keep only elements that match a condition.
list-filter.summary: LINQ Where creates a sequence of matching elements without modifying the original collection.
list-filter.why: Where applies the predicate to each element and enumerates only the elements for which it returns true.
list-filter.tips: Without ToList, remember that the result usually uses deferred execution.

list-sort.title: Sort a List
list-sort.short: Use Sort or OrderBy to change or produce an ordering.
list-sort.summary: List.Sort modifies the original List, while OrderBy returns a newly ordered sequence.
list-sort.why: Choose based on whether you want to mutate the original data or obtain a separate ordered view.
list-sort.tips: For multiple sort keys, chain OrderBy(...).ThenBy(...).

hashset-basic.title: Remove duplicates with HashSet<T>
hashset-basic.short: Keep at most one copy of each equal value.
hashset-basic.summary: HashSet<T> is useful when duplicates are not allowed and fast membership tests are important.
hashset-basic.why: HashSet<T> does not store multiple elements that are equal according to its comparer.
hashset-basic.tips: If you need stable ordering or index access, another structure such as List<T> may be more appropriate.

string-split-join.title: Split and join strings
string-split-join.short: Split text by a delimiter and join values again.
string-split-join.summary: These operations are common for simple delimited text and competitive-programming input processing.
string-split-join.why: Split turns a string into pieces, while Join combines multiple values with a separator.
string-split-join.tips: Real CSV with quoted fields cannot be parsed correctly with a simple Split alone.

string-interpolation.title: String interpolation
string-interpolation.summary: String interpolation inserts values and expressions without long chains of string concatenation.
string-interpolation.why: Expressions inside braces are evaluated and their results are formatted into the string.
string-interpolation.tips: Format specifiers are supported too, for example {value:N2}.

date-format.title: Format a DateTime for display
date-format.short: Use a ToString format string to control date and time output.
date-format.summary: You can convert year, month, day, time, and other components into the exact display format you need.
date-format.why: Format tokens such as yyyy, MM, and dd are replaced with the corresponding DateTime components.
date-format.tips: MM means month while mm means minutes, so letter case matters.

file-write.title: Write a text file
file-write.summary: This is the simplest way to save a small amount of text to a file in one operation.
file-write.why: File.WriteAllText handles opening, writing, and closing the file for you.
file-write.tips: Use File.AppendAllText when you want to add to existing content instead of replacing it.

directory-enumerate.title: Enumerate files in a directory
directory-enumerate.short: Use Directory.EnumerateFiles to receive file paths one by one.
directory-enumerate.summary: This is useful when processing many files from a folder.
directory-enumerate.why: EnumerateFiles yields paths as they are enumerated, which is convenient for directories containing many files.
directory-enumerate.tips: Pass a SearchOption when subdirectories should be included.

json-write.title: Convert an object to JSON
json-write.short: Use JsonSerializer.Serialize to turn a C# value into JSON text.
json-write.summary: System.Text.Json can serialize objects into JSON.
json-write.why: The serializer inspects public properties and other configured members and converts them to JSON values and objects.
json-write.tips: Combine this with File.WriteAllText when the JSON should be saved to disk.

http-get.title: Send a GET request with HttpClient
http-get.short: Retrieve data from the web with HTTP GET.
http-get.summary: HttpClient methods such as GetStringAsync can retrieve HTTP resources asynchronously.
http-get.why: Network operations involve waiting, so these APIs are exposed asynchronously.
http-get.tips: Real applications should also consider HttpClient lifetime, unsuccessful status codes, and cancellation.

regex-basic.title: Search text with a regular expression
regex-basic.short: Use Regex.IsMatch or Match to test a pattern.
regex-basic.summary: Regular expressions describe patterns for validating string formats or finding substrings.
regex-basic.why: The pattern \d+ matches a sequence of one or more digits.
regex-basic.tips: Very complicated regular expressions can become difficult to maintain; ordinary string operations may be clearer for simple cases.

task-delay.title: Wait asynchronously for a duration
task-delay.short: Await Task.Delay instead of blocking the thread.
task-delay.summary: Task.Delay waits asynchronously without occupying a thread with Thread.Sleep for the entire delay.
task-delay.why: Task.Delay returns a Task that completes after the requested duration.
task-delay.tips: Pass a CancellationToken when the delay should be cancellable.

cancellation-token.title: Cancel work with CancellationToken
cancellation-token.short: Pass a cancellation request into asynchronous or long-running work.
cancellation-token.summary: CancellationToken is the standard mechanism for telling an operation that its result is no longer needed.
cancellation-token.why: Cancellation is cooperative rather than forced: the operation checks the token at safe points and stops cleanly.
cancellation-token.tips: When a library method accepts a token, usually pass along the token you received instead of creating an unrelated one.

linq-select.title: Transform values with LINQ Select
linq-select.short: Map each element to another value and produce a new sequence.
linq-select.summary: Select applies the same transformation to every element of a sequence.
linq-select.why: For each x, the selector evaluates x * x and enumerates the resulting values in order.
linq-select.tips: Where filters elements; Select transforms them. They can be chained together.

linq-groupby.title: Group values with LINQ GroupBy
linq-groupby.short: Collect elements that share the same key.
linq-groupby.summary: GroupBy is useful for organizing data by values such as category, grade, or another key.
linq-groupby.why: Elements are grouped by the value returned from the key selector and exposed through IGrouping sequences.
linq-groupby.tips: For aggregation, combine GroupBy with Count, Sum, Select, and similar operators.

linq-distinct.title: Remove duplicates with Distinct
linq-distinct.short: Produce a sequence containing one copy of each equal value.
linq-distinct.summary: LINQ Distinct removes duplicate elements according to equality rules.
linq-distinct.why: Elements equal to values already seen are omitted from the result.
linq-distinct.tips: If you need to maintain a duplicate-free set over time, HashSet<T> may express the intent more directly.

try-catch.title: Handle exceptions with try / catch
try-catch.short: Catch expected failures and decide what to do when they occur.
try-catch.summary: Put code that may throw in try and handle specific recoverable exception types in catch.
try-catch.why: When an exception is thrown, normal control flow stops and execution transfers to a matching catch block.
try-catch.tips: Avoid swallowing every failure with catch (Exception); handle concrete exceptions only when you can respond meaningfully.

event-data-pattern.title: Passing notification data with EventHandler<T>
event-data-pattern.short: Publish typed event data together with the object that raised the notification.
event-data-pattern.summary: EventHandler<TEventArgs> standardizes a sender and event-data pair. The publisher raises the event, while subscribers attach and detach handlers without being able to invoke it directly.
event-data-pattern.why: Download supplies itself as sender and a ProgressEventArgs instance as data. Keeping the handler in a named variable makes -= remove the exact delegate that += added.
event-data-pattern.tips: The [[events|event]] boundary permits subscription but reserves notification for Download. Long-lived subscriptions should be removed or owned by an IDisposable lifetime when they are no longer needed.

queue-stack.title: Managing order with Queue<T> and Stack<T>
queue-stack.short: Choose FIFO or LIFO removal and handle an empty collection safely.
queue-stack.summary: Queue<T> removes the earliest enqueued item, while Stack<T> removes the most recently pushed item. TryDequeue and TryPop report an empty collection without throwing.
queue-stack.why: The queue prints Ada first and the stack prints second first, making the retrieval policy explicit.
queue-stack.tips: Viewing contents through [[ienumerable|IEnumerable]] only enumerates them; Dequeue, TryDequeue, Pop, and TryPop remove the next item.

priority-queue.title: Retrieving work with PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>
priority-queue.short: Remove the element whose independent priority compares smallest.
priority-queue.summary: PriorityQueue stores an element and priority separately. By default, the smallest priority is dequeued first, and equal priorities have no guaranteed relative order.
priority-queue.why: The alert has priority 5, so it leaves before both priority-20 jobs regardless of insertion order.
priority-queue.tips: A supplied [[custom-ordering|priority comparison]] controls removal order; add a tie-break component to the priority when equal-priority stability matters.

linked-list.title: Inserting around nodes with LinkedList<T>
linked-list.short: Retain a node to update adjacent positions without an index.
linked-list.summary: LinkedList<T> can insert or remove next to a known node in constant time, but finding a node by value or position still requires traversal.
linked-list.why: Keeping the Central node lets AddBefore, AddAfter, and Remove operate directly on its links.
linked-list.tips: Unlike [[list-basic|indexed List<T> operations]], linked nodes do not provide fast arbitrary index lookup; retain a node only while it belongs to that list.

immutable-collections.title: Keeping immutable snapshots with ImmutableArray<T>
immutable-collections.short: Derive a changed sequence without modifying the earlier value.
immutable-collections.summary: ImmutableArray<T> keeps a stable container snapshot. Add returns a new value, so first remains unchanged while second includes green.
immutable-collections.why: The immutable container cannot have its slots replaced, although a reference stored in a slot may still point to a mutable object.
immutable-collections.tips: This stable container differs from a live [[readonly-collection-views|read-only view]], which can reflect mutations performed by another owner.

dictionary-update-insert.title: Inserting, updating, and removing Dictionary entries
dictionary-update-insert.short: Select an operation whose duplicate-key policy matches the requirement.
dictionary-update-insert.summary: Add rejects a duplicate by throwing, TryAdd reports false, indexer assignment inserts or replaces, and Remove can report both success and the removed value.
dictionary-update-insert.why: Each operation makes a different policy visible instead of accidentally overwriting or rejecting data.
dictionary-update-insert.tips: Insertion policy is separate from [[dict-safe|safe key lookup]]; use TryGetValue when absence during reading is expected.

dictionary-comparers.title: Choosing Dictionary key comparers
dictionary-comparers.short: Apply one explicit equality policy to every key operation.
dictionary-comparers.summary: A comparer passed to the Dictionary constructor governs insertion, lookup, replacement, and removal for the lifetime of that dictionary.
dictionary-comparers.why: OrdinalIgnoreCase makes the three spellings of Content-Type the same key, so lookup succeeds and the duplicate TryAdd returns false.
dictionary-comparers.tips: A supplied comparer must obey the [[custom-equality-hashing|equality and hash-code contract]] so equal keys always receive compatible hash codes.

hashset-set-operations.title: Computing set unions, intersections, and differences
hashset-set-operations.short: Combine membership sets and test their relationships.
hashset-set-operations.summary: UnionWith, IntersectWith, and ExceptWith mutate their receiver. Copy the source first when the original set must remain unchanged.
hashset-set-operations.why: The three copied sets independently compute all members, common members, and members found only in first.
hashset-set-operations.tips: The [[hashset-basic|HashSet membership model]] uses its equality comparer for both operations and tests such as IsSubsetOf and Overlaps.

array-copy-clear.title: Copying and clearing array segments
array-copy-clear.short: Copy a bounded range and reset slots to their default values.
array-copy-clear.summary: Array.Copy copies a selected segment and correctly handles overlapping source and destination ranges. Array.Clear assigns default to each selected slot.
array-copy-clear.why: Copying an array of objects is shallow: target receives references to the same Box instances, while clearing target slots sets those references to null.
array-copy-clear.tips: Under [[value-reference-types|reference-type copying]], changing a copied object's state is visible through every reference to that object.

array-binary-search.title: Binary search in a sorted array
array-binary-search.short: Search ordered data and decode a missing value's insertion point.
array-binary-search.summary: Array.BinarySearch returns an index for a match. For a missing value it returns the bitwise complement of the index where that value could be inserted.
array-binary-search.why: Applying ~ to the negative result recovers the insertion index without performing a second scan.
array-binary-search.tips: The sort and search must use the same [[custom-ordering|comparison policy]]; otherwise binary search results are undefined.

list-removeall.title: Removing matching elements from a List<T>
list-removeall.short: Mutate a list with a predicate and receive the removed count.
list-removeall.summary: RemoveAll traverses the list, removes every matching element in place, and returns how many elements were removed.
list-removeall.why: The even values disappear from numbers itself, and removed records that three elements matched.
list-removeall.tips: Use [[list-filter|Where filtering]] when you need a separate filtered sequence instead of changing the original list.

linq-any-all.title: Testing sequence conditions with Any and All
linq-any-all.short: Test whether some or every element satisfies a predicate.
linq-any-all.summary: Any stops after the first success; All stops after the first failure. On an empty sequence Any is false, while All with a predicate is vacuously true.
linq-any-all.why: Neither operator needs to inspect later elements after its result has become certain.
linq-any-all.tips: Their short-circuit behavior follows the same idea as [[boolean-operators|short-circuit Boolean operators]], which skip work once the outcome is known.

linq-first-single.title: Expressing cardinality with First and Single
linq-first-single.short: Choose the operator that states how many matches are valid.
linq-first-single.summary: First accepts one or more matches and returns the first. Single requires exactly one; the non-OrDefault forms fail on no match, and Single also fails on multiple matches.
linq-first-single.why: Single expresses the unique-user contract, while SingleOrDefault permits absence but can be ambiguous when default(T) is itself a valid value.
linq-first-single.tips: A violated cardinality contract raises [[invalid-operation|InvalidOperationException]]; use nullable results, Any, or an explicit sentinel when default-value ambiguity matters.

linq-aggregate.title: Custom reductions with Aggregate
linq-aggregate.short: Fold sequence elements into an explicitly seeded accumulator.
linq-aggregate.summary: Aggregate passes the accumulated state and current element to a function, then uses its result as the state for the next element.
linq-aggregate.why: Because Topics: is an explicit seed, even an empty input has a defined result instead of requiring a first element.
linq-aggregate.tips: The [[lambda|accumulator function]] receives previous state first and the current element second; keep it free of surprising mutation when possible.

linq-sum-average.title: Computing sums and averages with LINQ
linq-sum-average.short: Aggregate numeric values directly or through a selector.
linq-sum-average.summary: Sum and Average have numeric overloads and selector overloads. Non-nullable Average throws on empty input, while nullable Average returns null when no values exist; nullable aggregates ignore null values.
linq-sum-average.why: The selector extracts each quantity. The nullable example excludes the missing value, producing 30 and an average of 15.
linq-sum-average.tips: Nullable inputs follow [[nullable-value-types|missing-value semantics]]. Sum of an empty numeric sequence is zero, and checked integer Sum overloads can throw OverflowException when the total is outside range.

linq-minby-maxby.title: Selecting extreme elements with MinBy and MaxBy
linq-minby-maxby.short: Return the element with the smallest or largest selected key.
linq-minby-maxby.summary: MinBy and MaxBy scan the sequence without sorting it and return a source element, not merely the selected key.
linq-minby-maxby.why: Price supplies the ordering key, so the complete Pen and Bag objects are returned in one pass.
linq-minby-maxby.tips: The selected key uses its default or supplied [[custom-ordering|ordering]]. Empty reference-type sources return null; empty non-nullable value-type sources throw InvalidOperationException.

linq-selectmany.title: Flattening nested sequences with SelectMany
linq-selectmany.short: Emit every child while optionally retaining its parent.
linq-selectmany.summary: Select produces one result for each input. SelectMany enumerates a child sequence for each input and flattens all child results into one sequence.
linq-selectmany.why: The result selector receives both the Department and each member, preserving the department name in every flattened result.
linq-selectmany.tips: Compare this with [[linq-select|Select's one-output-per-input transformation]] when choosing whether the result should remain nested or become flat.

linq-join.title: Joining sequences by matching keys
linq-join.short: Build in-memory inner-join rows for equal keys.
linq-join.summary: Join matches outer and inner keys. Unmatched elements produce no row, while one outer element can produce multiple rows when several inner elements share its key.
linq-join.why: Ada produces Book and Pen rows; Grace and the customer-3 order are omitted because an inner join has no match for them.
linq-join.tips: The result selector creates an [[anonymous-types|anonymous combined shape]] containing exactly the fields needed by later query stages.

linq-groupjoin.title: Grouping matches per parent with GroupJoin
linq-groupjoin.short: Associate every outer element with all matching inner elements.
linq-groupjoin.summary: GroupJoin returns one result for each outer element, including an empty group when no inner elements match. Flattening that group can implement a left join.
linq-groupjoin.why: DefaultIfEmpty contributes one null order for Grace's empty group, so SelectMany still emits the parent with a fallback item.
linq-groupjoin.tips: Use [[linq-defaultifempty|DefaultIfEmpty]] while flattening to retain unmatched parents; without it, an empty group contributes no row.

linq-pagination.title: Selecting pages with Skip and Take
linq-pagination.short: Validate a page request, compute its offset, and take a bounded slice.
linq-pagination.summary: Skip discards the requested prefix and Take emits at most the page size. The example rejects invalid values and uses checked arithmetic for the offset.
linq-pagination.why: A deterministic OrderBy makes page two consistently contain values 4 through 6, even if the source's original order changes.
linq-pagination.tips: Pagination needs a stable [[list-sort|ordering policy]]. On a general deferred IEnumerable, reaching a later page may still enumerate every preceding element.

linq-chunk.title: Batching sequence elements with Chunk
linq-chunk.short: Process source elements in arrays up to a chosen size.
linq-chunk.summary: Chunk enumerates the source into separate arrays whose maximum length is the requested chunk size. The final array can be shorter.
linq-chunk.why: Eight values with a size of three produce arrays of lengths three, three, and two.
linq-chunk.tips: Each result is an independent [[arrays-basics|array]] whose Length is its actual element count, not always the requested maximum.

linq-zip.title: Combining sequences positionally with Zip
linq-zip.short: Pair elements that occupy the same position.
linq-zip.summary: Zip advances its inputs together and stops as soon as the shortest input ends, so extra elements in longer inputs are omitted.
linq-zip.why: Only Ada and Grace receive scores because scores has two elements; Linus is never paired.
linq-zip.tips: Zip is positional, unlike a [[linq-join|key-based Join]]; choose Join when elements should match by identity rather than index.

linq-set-operators.title: Comparing sequences with LINQ set operators
linq-set-operators.short: Create duplicate-free unions, intersections, and differences.
linq-set-operators.summary: Union, Intersect, and Except return new deferred sequences and suppress duplicate members according to the supplied equality comparer.
linq-set-operators.why: OrdinalIgnoreCase treats Ada and ada as the same member consistently across all three operations.
linq-set-operators.tips: The comparer defines the [[equality|element equality contract]] that decides whether two values represent one set member.

linq-tolookup.title: Building a multi-value index with ToLookup
linq-tolookup.short: Materialize reusable groups addressable by key.
linq-tolookup.summary: ToLookup immediately builds a one-to-many index. Indexing a missing key returns an empty sequence rather than throwing.
linq-tolookup.why: Customer 1 can retrieve both orders repeatedly, while customer 99 produces a group with count zero.
linq-tolookup.tips: Unlike deferred [[linq-groupby|GroupBy enumeration]], ToLookup materializes now and is convenient for repeated keyed access to the captured data.

linq-cast-oftype.title: Producing typed sequences with Cast and OfType
linq-cast-oftype.short: Choose strict conversion or type-based filtering for mixed elements.
linq-cast-oftype.summary: Cast<T> attempts to cast every element, and Cast<string?> preserves compatible nulls. OfType<T> filters null for every T, including nullable and reference targets, and emits only non-null elements assignable to T.
linq-cast-oftype.why: OfType<int> keeps 1 and 3. The compatible Cast example accepts strings and null, but adding an int would fail when enumeration reaches it.
linq-cast-oftype.tips: Because Cast is deferred, an incompatible element raises [[invalid-cast|InvalidCastException]] during enumeration rather than when the query is created.

linq-sequenceequal.title: Comparing ordered contents with SequenceEqual
linq-sequenceequal.short: Compare element values and positions under one equality policy.
linq-sequenceequal.summary: SequenceEqual advances both sequences together and requires equal lengths and equal elements in the same order.
linq-sequenceequal.why: The case-insensitive comparer makes the ordered contents equal even though the two array objects have different identities.
linq-sequenceequal.tips: SequenceEqual consumes an [[equality|element equality contract]]; it differs from set equality because duplicates and order remain significant.

linq-defaultifempty.title: Supplying an element for an empty sequence with DefaultIfEmpty
linq-defaultifempty.short: Yield one fallback only when the source has no elements.
linq-defaultifempty.summary: DefaultIfEmpty passes through a nonempty source unchanged. For an empty source it yields either the explicit fallback or default(T) exactly once.
linq-defaultifempty.why: The empty integer array produces -1 when supplied and zero when no explicit value is given; a source containing 5 keeps 5.
linq-defaultifempty.tips: The implicit fallback follows [[default-values|default(T)]]. One fallback row supports left joins and can deliberately change how downstream aggregation treats emptiness.

string-search-replace.title: Searching and replacing string content
string-search-replace.short: Find literal tokens and replace text under an explicit comparison rule.
string-search-replace.summary: IndexOf returns -1 when a literal is absent, and Replace returns a new string because strings are immutable. Both operations can state how text is compared.
string-search-replace.why: The token is an identifier, so [[string-comparison|an ordinal comparison policy]] is explicit rather than culture-dependent.
string-search-replace.tips: Check the not-found result before slicing. Use regular expressions only when the search requirement is actually pattern-based.

string-trim-validation.title: Distinguishing empty and whitespace text when normalizing input
string-trim-validation.short: Validate missing content before trimming the permitted boundaries.
string-trim-validation.summary: IsNullOrWhiteSpace handles null, empty, and all-whitespace input. Trim then removes whitespace only from the beginning and end, leaving interior content unchanged.
string-trim-validation.why: The [[nullable|null case]] must be handled before calling an instance string method.
string-trim-validation.tips: Define the input contract: Trim() recognizes Unicode whitespace, while Trim with selected characters is appropriate when only specific boundary characters are allowed.

stringbuilder.title: Building text incrementally with StringBuilder
stringbuilder.short: Accumulate many fragments without creating a new string at each step.
stringbuilder.summary: StringBuilder keeps a mutable character buffer for repeated appends, and ToString creates the final immutable string.
stringbuilder.why: A loop can append separators and values efficiently, while [[string-interpolation|ordinary interpolation]] remains clearer for one small formatted message.
stringbuilder.tips: Do not introduce StringBuilder for a handful of fixed concatenations. Call ToString at the boundary where an actual string is required.

unicode-normalization.title: Normalizing equivalent Unicode representations
unicode-normalization.short: Align canonically equivalent scalar sequences before comparison.
unicode-normalization.summary: Normalization Form C composes canonically equivalent sequences into a consistent representation, allowing a suitable comparison policy to recognize equivalent text.
unicode-normalization.why: The same visible text can contain different [[unicode-runes|Unicode scalar sequences]], such as one precomposed scalar or a base scalar followed by a combining mark.
unicode-normalization.tips: Normalization does not remove accents and does not make unrelated lookalike characters equal. Normalize at a documented boundary and then apply the intended comparison rule.

span-parse.title: Parsing text spans without substring allocation
span-parse.short: Pass a bounded view directly to a span-aware parser.
span-parse.summary: AsSpan creates a ReadOnlySpan<char> over part of the original string, and numeric TryParse overloads can consume that view without allocating a temporary substring.
span-parse.why: The token [[span-memory|shares the original text storage]], so its valid lifetime is tied to that source.
span-parse.tips: Validate slice boundaries and state NumberStyles and culture. Prefer clarity over allocation avoidance unless parsing is a measured hot path.

base64.title: Representing binary data as Base64 text
base64.short: Round-trip bytes through a text-safe representation and reject malformed input.
base64.summary: Base64 maps arbitrary bytes to printable text and back. FromBase64String throws FormatException for invalid alphabet, padding, or length.
base64.why: After decoding, arbitrary binary remains bytes. Only if the original producer encoded text should the recovered bytes be decoded with that same [[encoding-text-bytes|text encoding]].
base64.tips: Base64 is encoding, not encryption or integrity protection, and usually increases size by roughly one third.

regex-groups.title: Extracting fields with named regular-expression groups
regex-groups.short: Read structured fields by name after confirming a bounded match succeeded.
regex-groups.summary: Named captures make fields explicit. Match.Success says the entire pattern matched, while Group.Success distinguishes an optional group that did not participate from one that captured an empty value.
regex-groups.why: Check [[regex-basic|match success]] before consuming any captured fields.
regex-groups.tips: Keep parsing separate from matching: validate or TryParse captured numeric text after extraction, and always use a finite timeout.

regex-replace.title: Replacing text with regular-expression transformations
regex-replace.short: Transform repeated matches with captures or a MatchEvaluator.
regex-replace.summary: Regex.Replace can substitute capture references in replacement text or invoke a MatchEvaluator for computed output. Replacement syntax is distinct from pattern syntax.
regex-replace.why: The evaluator receives each Match and can read the values exposed by [[regex-groups|named capture groups]].
regex-replace.tips: Use a literal string Replace for literal work. When replacement text comes from users, do not assume pattern escaping also makes replacement syntax literal.

date-parse-exact.title: Parsing dates with an exact format
date-parse-exact.short: Accept one documented date-time shape with explicit culture and styles.
date-parse-exact.summary: TryParseExact succeeds only when input conforms to the supplied format, culture, and DateTimeStyles, avoiding the ambiguity of broad culture-dependent parsing.
date-parse-exact.why: The [[date-format|format tokens]] used for output must match the intended input contract; yyyy-MM-dd differs from culture-specific short-date patterns.
date-parse-exact.tips: A parsed wall-clock value with no offset remains Unspecified. Choose a zone or offset explicitly before treating it as an instant.

time-zone-conversion.title: Converting time zones with TimeZoneInfo
time-zone-conversion.short: Convert a known instant and validate local wall-clock times at transitions.
time-zone-conversion.summary: ConvertTime maps an unambiguous instant into a selected zone. A local wall-clock input can be invalid during a forward jump or ambiguous during a backward transition and needs an application policy.
time-zone-conversion.why: A [[datetimeoffset|DateTimeOffset input]] supplies the unambiguous instant used for zone conversion.
time-zone-conversion.tips: Time-zone identifiers and installed rule data vary by environment; configure and validate the intended zone instead of claiming one arbitrary ID is universally portable.

timespan-arithmetic.title: Calculating durations with TimeSpan
timespan-arithmetic.short: Construct, combine, and subtract elapsed quantities in a stated time basis.
timespan-arithmetic.summary: TimeSpan represents a duration. Compatible timestamps can be subtracted to obtain one, and durations can be added or subtracted without implying calendar rules.
timespan-arithmetic.why: Two [[datetimeoffset|DateTimeOffset values]] identify instants suitable for elapsed-time subtraction after their basis is understood.
timespan-arithmetic.tips: A month or local calendar day is not a fixed TimeSpan. Apply calendar arithmetic to the calendar type and zone rules instead.

stopwatch.title: Measuring execution time with Stopwatch
stopwatch.short: Measure elapsed work with a monotonic timing source.
stopwatch.summary: Stopwatch is designed for elapsed measurement and avoids civil-clock adjustments that can affect DateTime.Now subtraction.
stopwatch.why: Elapsed is returned as a [[timespan-arithmetic|TimeSpan duration]], with TotalMilliseconds available for reporting.
stopwatch.tips: Warm-up, scheduling, runtime optimization, and noise affect small samples. Repeat measurements and report only precision the experiment supports.

math-rounding.title: Choosing rounding, floor, ceiling, and truncation
math-rounding.short: Select a boundary rule explicitly for both positive and negative values.
math-rounding.summary: Round applies a midpoint policy, Floor moves toward negative infinity, Ceiling toward positive infinity, and Truncate toward zero.
math-rounding.why: A cast performs a [[numeric-conversions|numeric conversion]] that truncates floating or decimal values toward zero; it is not a substitute for every rounding policy.
math-rounding.tips: State MidpointRounding at domain boundaries. Test negative values and exact midpoints because intuitive positive-only examples hide important differences.

math-clamp.title: Bounding values with Math.Clamp, Min, and Max
math-clamp.short: Normalize finite values to a validated interval or reject them by policy.
math-clamp.summary: Math.Clamp returns the lower bound, upper bound, or original in-range value. Min and Max combine individual bounds but do not replace validation.
math-clamp.why: Math.Clamp throws [[argument-exception|ArgumentException]] when the minimum bound exceeds the maximum bound.
math-clamp.tips: Reject NaN or infinity when the domain requires finite values. Clamping invalid user input can conceal an error, so distinguish normalization from validation.

random-generation.title: Controlling random ranges and reproducibility
random-generation.short: Respect exclusive upper bounds and seed examples that must replay.
random-generation.summary: Random.Next(min, max) includes min and excludes max. A fixed seed reproduces a deterministic sequence for tests and demonstrations.
random-generation.why: The requested range must fit the destination [[numeric-types|numeric type]] and its API bounds.
random-generation.tips: Random is not cryptographically secure. Use RandomNumberGenerator for secrets, tokens, or adversarial settings, and do not reseed repeatedly inside a loop.

random-shuffle-sampling.title: Shuffling arrays and sampling without replacement
random-shuffle-sampling.short: Shuffle an owned array and take a unique prefix.
random-shuffle-sampling.summary: Random.Shuffle mutates the supplied span or array. Shuffling a copy and taking its first k elements samples without replacement while preserving the source.
random-shuffle-sampling.why: Independent [[random-generation|random index draws]] can select the same element more than once, so they do not guarantee a unique sample.
random-shuffle-sampling.tips: Random.Shuffle is available in .NET 8. Validate that k is within the array bounds and use a cryptographic design when unpredictability is a security requirement.

guid.title: Creating and parsing identifiers with Guid
guid.short: Treat GUIDs as opaque identifiers with a stable textual format.
guid.summary: Guid.NewGuid creates an identifier, TryParseExact validates external text against a chosen format, and ToString with the same format gives a stable representation.
guid.why: A parsed identifier can be a stable [[dictionary-update-insert|dictionary key]] because Guid has value equality and hashing.
guid.tips: A Guid is neither a secret nor a meaningful chronological ordering. Validate the accepted format rather than relying on permissive parsing when the contract is fixed.

biginteger.title: Calculating large integers with BigInteger
biginteger.short: Perform exact integer arithmetic beyond fixed-width ranges.
biginteger.summary: BigInteger grows as needed instead of wrapping at Int32 or Int64 boundaries, but larger values consume increasing memory and processing time.
biginteger.why: The factorial avoids the fixed-width limit that causes [[integer-overflow|integer overflow]].
biginteger.tips: Conversions back to fixed-width types still have boundaries and can throw OverflowException. BigInteger is arbitrary precision, not unlimited resources.

decimal-calculations.title: Making decimal arithmetic and rounding explicit
decimal-calculations.short: Keep decimal quantities decimal and round once at a defined boundary.
decimal-calculations.summary: decimal represents base-10-scaled values with finite precision. Decimal literals and intermediates avoid introducing binary floating-point approximations into the calculation.
decimal-calculations.why: A binary floating-point intermediate can undermine a decimal workflow through the approximation behavior described by [[floating-equality|floating-point equality]].
decimal-calculations.tips: Define when and how to round, retain unrounded intermediates when the domain requires it, and do not claim decimal has unlimited precision or range.
